title: Canada keeps rates steady as new tariffs put a broader recovery at risk
summary: The Bank of Canada left its overnight target at 2.25% on 2 September. Its Bank Rate was 2.50% and its deposit rate 2.20%. A stronger Canadian economy and headline inflation near 3% had not yet displaced Governing Council’s July baseline. What had changed was the distribution of risks. Energy costs remained high, refinery margins were elevated and little progress had been made towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Canada–US trade talks had broken down, with new US tariffs and Canadian countermeasures announced. Council saw a greater risk of persistent inflation alongside more uncertainty about whether the recovery could last. Neither the extent of renewed trade restrictions nor the duration of the energy shock was settled.

The domestic data provided stronger evidence of recovery than an isolated output rebound. Second-quarter GDP rose 3.3% after a very weak first quarter; consumption made solid gains, housing rebounded after a run of weak quarters, and exports and business investment rose sharply. Some temporary reversals still contributed. The coexistence of broad gains and temporary support matters: breadth lends weight to the recovery, while composition limits what can safely be extrapolated. July unemployment had edged down to 6.4% and other labour conditions had improved, but hiring demand remained subdued. Council still saw unused capacity. One strong quarter could thus reduce the risk of a prolonged contraction without establishing that demand had already overtaken supply.

The prospective tariff shock complicates each component differently. A US tariff on Canadian products could weaken orders and delay investment in exposed sectors. Canadian counter-tariffs could raise the cost of imported inputs for domestic firms, with the effect on final prices depending on margins and substitution. The release reported announcement of the measures and exposure to further action. It did not provide rates, detailed sector weights or a quantified hit to GDP. Treating every export change in the second-quarter data as a reaction to these new announcements would invert the sequence of events. The immediate research question was which parts of the existing recovery had enough domestic or non-US demand to be sustained if trade costs rose.

Headline prices had hovered around 3% in recent months, largely because gasoline remained expensive. In July, inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% and core measures stayed near 2%. Thus the realised evidence still pointed to limited spread beyond fuel. Council nevertheless raised its assessment of upside inflation risk. A prolonged shock changes the economics of absorption: a firm can temporarily accept a lower margin on a delivery contract, but may revise the contract price if fuel and other input costs are likely to stay high. Elevated refinery margins also mean crude oil alone is an incomplete indicator of the price paid by fuel users. New tariffs could add pricing pressure distinct from energy. Council did not present evidence that these spillovers were already widespread.

Market developments before the decision were also mixed. Long-term yields had risen globally, including in Canada, and financial conditions had tightened since July. The Canadian dollar appreciated slightly as the US dollar weakened. A higher Canadian yield need not therefore mark a change in the expected domestic policy target, and the modest currency appreciation did not guarantee lower domestic fuel costs. The external backdrop included stronger-than-expected euro-area activity, slower growth in China and continued US consumption and AI investment. The Bank judged overall global growth broadly in line with July. By holding, Council left the next policy choice dependent on whether the rebound endured and whether costs began spreading through the inflation basket. It did not supply an announcement-window measure of the market’s response.

questions.question: Which parts of the recovery were exposed to the newly announced tariffs?
questions.detail: Break down exports and investment by industry and destination, aligning orders and shipments to announcement and effective dates. Canada’s second-quarter growth predates the new measures, so distinguish the underlying rebound from subsequent stockpiling or cancellations. Less-exposed domestic spending and investment can provide a comparison when judging the durability of the recovery.

questions.question: Were elevated refinery margins increasing pass-through beyond the fuel component?
questions.detail: Track refined-products prices separately from crude, then examine transport-intensive producer and consumer prices, firms’ margins and survey pricing plans. Look for changes in breadth and frequency of increases while allowing for tariff exposure. This would test whether 2.2% inflation excluding gasoline still captured underlying pressure or lagged scheduled price resets.

questions.question: Did higher Canadian long yields tighten borrowing costs independently of domestic policy expectations?
questions.detail: Compare sovereign yields with matched US maturities, shorter Canadian meeting-sensitive rates and spreads on private borrowing. Examine mortgage and business lending rates over the same dates. A synchronised global duration move would transmit differently from an expected domestic hike even if the observed change in a benchmark Canadian bond yield were identical. Compare fixed and floating lending rates separately, since the businesses facing trade exposure may not refinance on the same schedule.
